title: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition) · Units 11–12
description: Confusable verbs for gains, competitions, clothing and time, plus figurative collocations based on light, water, fire and emotion.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the supplied edition. Short learning targets follow the source units and exercises; all translations, notes and teaching sentences are newly written. Original textbook passages and exercise prompts are not reproduced.

units.title: Unit 11 — Synonyms and confusable words 2
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 26–27 (PDF pages 30–31).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Special aspects of collocation · gaining, winning and confusing verbs
learningObjectives: Choose gain, win, earn, make, achieve, beat and defeat with their natural noun partners.
Distinguish winning a competition from beating or defeating a competitor.
Distinguish take, carry, wear and use according to transport, possession, clothing and operation.
Use spend for time and money and avoid common incorrect verb substitutions.

items.section: A · Gain: authority, access and benefits
items.example: The coalition hopes to gain power after the election.
items.note: Gain power refers to acquiring political or organisational authority.

items.section: A · Gain: authority, access and benefits
items.example: The new team managed to gain control of the project.
items.note: Gain control means obtain the ability to direct or manage something.

items.section: A · Gain: authority, access and benefits
items.example: Visitors must register to gain access to the laboratory.
items.note: Gain access commonly takes to before the resource or place being accessed.

items.section: A · Gain: authority, access and benefits
items.example: The company gained a reputation for reliable equipment.
items.note: Gain a reputation for something describes developing a public image over time.

items.section: A · Gain: authority, access and benefits
items.example: The charity gained publicity after the local newspaper covered its work.
items.note: Publicity is public attention, not necessarily approval; gain is common in relatively formal writing.

items.section: A · Gain: authority, access and benefits
items.example: The young researcher gained recognition for her innovative design.
items.note: Recognition means being noticed or acknowledged for achievements.

items.section: A · Gain: authority, access and benefits
items.example: The runners gained an advantage by choosing a shorter route.
items.note: Gain an advantage often takes over to identify a competitor.

items.pt: ganhar um prêmio; receber uma premiação
items.example: The engineer hopes to win an award for her research.
items.note: Win is used for competitive recognition, such as an award.

items.example: Our school won a prize in the science competition.
items.note: A prize is awarded in a competition; do not use gain a prize in this ordinary sense.

items.example: He trained for years to win a medal at the championships.
items.note: Win describes the result of a competitive event.

items.example: The home team needs to win a match to reach the final.
items.note: You win a match but beat a team or an opponent.

items.example: The army managed to win a battle despite its smaller numbers.
items.note: Win is natural with battle; beat usually needs an opponent.

items.example: Both sides believed they could win a war quickly.
items.note: Win takes the conflict as its object, not the people defeated.

items.example: She hopes to win an election to the local council.
items.note: Win an election refers to electoral success; a party can also gain power.

items.example: The junior team was delighted to win a trophy this season.
items.note: A trophy is a competitive award; an exercise practises this pairing.

items.pt: receber um salário; ganhar um salário
items.example: Experienced technicians can earn a salary that reflects their qualifications.
items.note: Earn a salary normally means receive regular pay for work.

items.example: She earns money by teaching evening classes.
items.note: Earn emphasises income from work, unlike make money, which can also involve investment.

items.example: The firm hopes to make money from its new service.
items.note: Make money can refer to income from business or investments, not just a salary.

items.example: The start-up expects to make a profit next year.
items.note: A business makes a profit when income exceeds costs; contrast make a loss.

items.example: The company made a loss in its first year of trading.
items.note: British English business expression for spending more than is earned; contrasted with make a profit in the exercise.

items.example: Small businesses can achieve success by understanding their customers.
items.note: Achieve combines with an abstract outcome rather than a competitive prize.

items.example: Regular practice will help you achieve your goals.
items.note: Goals are intended results; use achieve, not win, with this meaning.

items.pt: atingir suas metas; alcançar seus objetivos
items.example: The charity needs more volunteers to achieve its aims.
items.note: Aims means desired purposes or objectives; the expression is common in formal contexts.

items.pt: realizar uma ambição de longa data
items.example: She finally achieved a lifelong ambition when she published her first novel.
items.note: A lifelong ambition is a goal held for many years; used in the answer-key correction.

items.example: She hopes to beat an opponent who has never lost at home.
items.note: Beat requires the person or side defeated; win takes the match or competition.

items.example: He worked hard to defeat an opponent with more experience.
items.note: Defeat is somewhat more formal than beat, and both take an opponent.

items.pt: vencer um time; derrotar uma equipe
items.example: Our club managed to beat a team from the top division.
items.note: Beat a team, but win a game or match.

items.example: The visitors will try to defeat a team with a strong defence.
items.note: Defeat is a more formal alternative to beat for a team or opponent.

items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: Please take warm clothes because the nights can be cold.
items.note: Take emphasises bringing an item to a destination; carry emphasises transporting it.

items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: Most hikers carry a mobile phone in case of an emergency.
items.note: Carry means keep something with you, not wear it.

items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: You should wear a hat to protect your head from the sun.
items.note: Wear is used for clothes and accessories on your body; carry is different.

items.pt: carregar uma bolsa; carregar uma sacola
items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: Could you carry a bag for me while I open the door?
items.note: Carry means hold or transport the bag, not wear it.

items.pt: vestir um vestido; estar usando vestido
items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: She plans to wear a dress to the ceremony.
items.note: For clothes, use wear rather than use or carry.

items.pt: usar um notebook; utilizar um computador portátil
items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: He prefers to use a laptop when he travels.
items.note: Use is the normal verb for operating a device, rather than wear.

items.pt: usar um casaco; estar de casaco
items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: You will need to wear a coat outside this evening.
items.note: Wear describes having clothing on your body; take a coat means bring it along.

items.pt: vestir um terno; usar traje social
items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: He usually has to wear a suit at formal events.
items.note: Use wear, not use, for clothing.

items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: It is safer to stop walking before you use a mobile phone to read a map.
items.note: Use emphasises operating the phone; carry one means having it with you.

items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: You may need to use an umbrella if it rains later.
items.note: Use an umbrella describes its function; carry an umbrella describes transporting it.

items.section: B · Take, carry, wear and use
items.example: The consultant had to carry a briefcase full of documents.
items.note: Carry, not wear, describes holding or transporting a briefcase.

items.example: We decided to spend three days in the countryside.
items.note: Spend describes a period of time used in an activity or place, not pass three days.

items.example: Drivers may spend money on petrol each week.
items.note: Use spend money on for the thing you buy; do not substitute use money.

items.pt: passar duas horas assistindo à televisão
items.example: They sometimes spend two hours watching TV after dinner.
items.note: Use spend + time + -ing to describe the activity during that period.

items.word: spend an hour looking for something
items.pt: passar uma hora procurando alguma coisa
items.example: I had to spend an hour looking for something important in the archive.
items.note: After spend + time, an -ing clause names the activity; not pass or stay an hour.

items.pt: passar as férias; passar um período de férias
items.example: We plan to spend a holiday in a quiet coastal village.
items.note: Spend a holiday refers to where or how you use holiday time; the exercise contrasts pass.

items.pt: passar uma semana visitando pontos turísticos
items.example: I would love to spend a week sightseeing in Edinburgh.
items.note: Spend + period + -ing is the natural pattern for time devoted to an activity.

units.title: Unit 12 — Metaphor
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 28–29 (PDF pages 32–33).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Special aspects of collocation · figurative language and metaphor
learningObjectives: Recognise light and darkness as figurative ways of describing moods, emotions and hope.
Use flow, pour, stream, trickle and flood to describe speech, crowds, traffic and tears.
Interpret heated, fiery, flare up, burn and blaze in emotional or figurative contexts.
Identify metaphorical adjective–noun combinations involving bright, warm and cold.

items.example: Her sunny smile helped everyone relax before the meeting.
items.note: Sunny describes cheerful expression figuratively, not actual sunlight.

items.example: His sunny face reassured the younger children.
items.note: Sunny metaphorically suggests warmth and happiness in appearance.

items.example: Her face shines with pleasure whenever she talks about her new job.
items.note: Shine with pleasure is a figurative description of visible delight.

items.example: His eyes shine with excitement when he discusses astronomy.
items.note: Shine with names an emotion visibly expressed in the eyes.

items.example: The children’s eyes shine with delight when they see the decorations.
items.note: Delight is strong pleasure; shining eyes are figurative, not a literal light source.

items.example: Her face lights up whenever she sees her grandchildren.
items.note: Light up describes a sudden visible change towards happiness.

items.example: His eyes light up when someone mentions his favourite book.
items.note: Eyes light up means an immediate, noticeable expression of joy.

items.pt: descontrair o ambiente; aliviar o clima
items.example: A little humour can lighten the atmosphere during a difficult meeting.
items.note: Lighten makes a serious or tense social atmosphere more relaxed.

items.pt: melhorar o clima; deixar o ambiente mais leve
items.example: The host told a joke to lighten the mood.
items.note: Lighten the mood changes the emotional tone towards cheerfulness.

items.example: He struggled with dark thoughts after the unsettling news.
items.note: Dark metaphorically suggests gloomy or troubling ideas.

items.example: The town endured dark days during the crisis.
items.note: Dark days means an unpleasant or distressing period, not merely days without sunlight.

items.example: Friends supported each other through dark times.
items.note: Dark times is a figurative expression for periods of hardship.

items.example: His face darkens whenever he hears about the incident.
items.note: Darkens can describe an expression changing to anger or sadness.

items.pt: olhar fica sombrio; os olhos demonstram tristeza ou raiva
items.example: Her eyes darken when the subject of the argument comes up.
items.note: Eyes darken is figurative: the person’s expression changes negatively.

items.pt: expressão se fecha; semblante fica sombrio
items.example: The director’s expression darkens as the disappointing figures appear.
items.note: Darken signals a visible change towards displeasure, anger or sadness.

items.example: The young scientist seems to have a bright future ahead of her.
items.note: Bright suggests a hopeful, successful future rather than literal light.

items.example: Her teachers described her as a bright child who learns quickly.
items.note: Bright figuratively means intelligent, not a colour or light level.

items.example: The visitors received a warm welcome from the local community.
items.note: Warm means friendly and welcoming in this metaphor.

items.example: A warm smile from the receptionist made the guests feel comfortable.
items.note: Warm metaphorically suggests kindness and friendliness.

items.pt: olhar frio; olhos sem expressão acolhedora
items.example: He listened with cold eyes and said nothing.
items.note: Cold eyes suggests an unfriendly or emotionally distant gaze.

items.example: She gave him a cold stare after the rude remark.
items.note: Cold metaphorically signals an unfriendly, distant attitude.

items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: Ideas flow more easily when everyone feels comfortable speaking.
items.note: Flow suggests thoughts emerging smoothly without interruption.

items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: Conversation flows naturally when both people listen carefully.
items.note: Flow suggests effortless, continuous communication.

items.pt: uma enxurrada de lágrimas; choro intenso
items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: The farewell brought a flood of tears from the audience.
items.note: Flood figuratively describes a large amount of tears.

items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: She arrived home in floods of tears after the upsetting call.
items.note: This fixed British expression means crying heavily.

items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: After the reunion, tears stream down her face as she speaks.
items.note: Stream down evokes a continuous flow of tears; his or their may replace her.

items.pt: as pessoas saem em grande quantidade
items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: People pour out of the theatre when the show finishes.
items.note: Pour out means a large number of people leave rapidly and continuously.

items.pt: as pessoas entram em um prédio em fluxo contínuo
items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: People stream into a building as the doors open for the event.
items.note: Stream into highlights a continuous flow of many people.

items.pt: as pessoas entram aos poucos em um salão
items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: People trickle into a hall long before the talk begins.
items.note: Trickle indicates a small number arriving gradually, unlike pour or stream.

items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: The exhibition attracted a stream of visitors throughout the afternoon.
items.note: Stream of conveys an ongoing movement of people.

items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: A stream of traffic moved past the railway station.
items.note: Traffic is treated as a continuing flow, not as literal water.

items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: A steady stream of vehicles crossed the bridge all morning.
items.note: Steady strengthens the idea of an uninterrupted flow; practised in an exercise.

items.section: B · Water: flow, crowds and tears
items.example: By midnight, only a trickle of vehicles was entering the car park.
items.note: Trickle means relatively few vehicles arriving slowly; contrasted with a steady stream.

items.section: C · Fire and heat: anger and intensity
items.example: A heated debate followed the council’s proposal.
items.note: Heated suggests strong disagreement, often involving anger.

items.section: C · Fire and heat: anger and intensity
items.example: The committee had a heated discussion about the budget.
items.note: Heated describes emotional disagreement, not temperature.

items.section: C · Fire and heat: anger and intensity
items.example: They had a heated conversation about the new rules.
items.note: Heated marks a conversation in which people strongly disagree.

items.section: C · Fire and heat: anger and intensity
items.example: His fiery temper sometimes makes teamwork difficult.
items.note: Fiery temper describes a person who becomes angry very quickly.

items.section: C · Fire and heat: anger and intensity
items.example: Tempers flare when the deadline changes at the last minute.
items.note: Flare figuratively describes a sudden rise in anger among people.

items.pt: a violência irrompe novamente; a violência se intensifica de repente
items.section: C · Fire and heat: anger and intensity
items.example: Violence flares up again after several months of calm.
items.note: Flare up describes a sudden outbreak or renewal of an existing problem.

items.pt: os problemas ressurgem; os conflitos voltam a se intensificar
items.section: C · Fire and heat: anger and intensity
items.example: Troubles flare up whenever the rival groups meet.
items.note: Troubles refers to conflicts or unrest; flare up means become serious again.

items.pt: bochechas queimam de vergonha; rosto fica vermelho de constrangimento
items.section: C · Fire and heat: anger and intensity
items.example: Her cheeks burn with embarrassment when she remembers the mistake.
items.note: Burn is figurative for an intense feeling of embarrassment.

items.pt: um momento de glória espetacular; grande apogeu
items.section: C · Fire and heat: anger and intensity
items.example: The athlete ended her career in a blaze of glory.
items.note: Blaze of glory means an impressive, conspicuous success or triumphant moment.

items.pt: enorme repercussão na mídia; grande exposição pública
items.section: C · Fire and heat: anger and intensity
items.example: The launch was accompanied by a blaze of publicity.
items.note: Blaze of publicity means a great deal of striking public attention.
